title: Superior Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion (BRVO): Masterclass
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to the second most common retinal vascular disorder. Focuses on the pathophysiology of AV crossings, evidence-based management of macular edema, and the prevention of sight-threatening neovascular complications.

branches: Compression: Shared adventitial sheath at AV crossing
Stasis: Turbulent blood flow & endothelial damage

sections.title: 90D Lens Examination Technique
content: Step 1: Patient Setup: Dilate with Tropicamide 1% and Phenylephrine 2.5%. Ensure the room is dark.
Step 2: Alignment: Use a thin slit-beam. Pivot the lens to catch the red reflex. Adjust for the 1.0x (90D) magnification/inversion.
Step 3: Superior-Temporal Sweep: Move the joystick towards the patient's superior-temporal quadrant (Note: Image is inverted/reversed).
Step 4: Sign Identification: Look for the 'wedge-shaped' distribution of hemorrhages radiating from an AV crossing point.
Step 5: Foveal Assessment: Assess for thickening, loss of foveal reflex, or hard exudates (Macular Edema).

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Segmental 'Flame-shaped' intraretinal hemorrhages
Dilated and tortuous retinal veins distal to occlusion
Cotton-wool spots (suggesting focal ischemia)
Retinal edema (intracellular and extracellular)
Hard exudates (chronic edema manifestation)
Collateral vessels (develop over 6-12 months crossing the horizontal raphe)

rows: < 5 disc areas of non-perfusion on FFA
> 5 disc areas of non-perfusion on FFA
Can be present if large area involved
Guarded; high risk of Vitreous Hemorrhage

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: 1. Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT): Quantify Central Macular Thickness (CMT) and detect Subretinal Fluid (SRF).
2. Fluorescein Angiography (FFA): Identify areas of capillary non-perfusion, leakage (edema), and NVE.
3. Systemic Workup: Blood Pressure, Fasting Glucose, Lipid Profile.
4. Young Patient Screen: Protein C/S, Antithrombin III, Factor V Leiden, Homocysteine.

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Initial Assessment: If VA < 20/40 and ME is present, initiate Anti-VEGF therapy.
Anti-VEGF Regimen: Monthly injections (Aflibercept 2mg or Ranibizumab 0.5mg) for 3-6 months, then Treat-and-Extend.
Steroid Alternative: Dexamethasone implant (Ozurdex) for pseudophakic patients or those unresponsive to Anti-VEGF.
Observation: If VA is good and ME is minimal, monitor monthly for the first 4 months.
Laser Therapy: Perform Sectoral Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP) ONLY if neovascularization (NVD/NVE) develops.

rows: Argon laser grid photocoagulation beneficial for ME with VA 20/40 to 20/200 after 3-6 months.
Ranibizumab significantly improved VA compared to sham for BRVO-associated ME.
Aflibercept superior to grid laser at 24 weeks for VA improvement.
Dexamethasone implant (Ozurdex) effective but carries risk of IOP spike and Cataract.
Triamcinolone 1mg equal to laser but with more side effects.

sections.title: Complications & Red Flags
content: Neovascularization of the Disc (NVD) or Elsewhere (NVE)
Vitreous Hemorrhage (Sudden new floaters/vision loss)
Tractional Retinal Detachment (TRD)
Neovascular Glaucoma (Rare in BRVO vs CRVO, but possible)
Chronic Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) leading to foveal atrophy

content.explanation: B: Blood Pressure control is priority. R: Radial wedge of hemorrhages. V: VEGF inhibitors are 1st line. O: Observe for Ischemia/NV.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Collateral vessels: Do NOT laser them! They are physiological bypasses that help drain the retina.
Macular Ischemia: If VA is poor despite resolved edema on OCT, check FFA for Enlarged Foveal Avascular Zone (FAZ).
The 90-Day Rule: Historically for CRVO, but in BRVO, monitor for NV most closely in the first 6-12 months.
Inverted View: When using 90D, a superior-temporal BRVO appears inferior-nasal through the lens.
Bilateral BRVO: Always prompt a workup for systemic hypercoagulability or vasculitis.
